Setting up the lab…

Protein Synthesis 3D Lab

Your DNA holds the recipes for every protein in your body, from the enzymes that digest your lunch to the hemoglobin that carries your oxygen. Copy a gene into mRNA, read it at a ribosome and build the protein one amino acid at a time. Then change a single DNA base to see how a tiny mistake can do nothing, or cause a disease like sickle cell. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

🧬 The central idea

DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein

The order of bases in a gene sets the order of amino acids in a protein. Three bases (one codon) code for one amino acid.

✏️ Why one letter matters

GAG → GTG Glu → Val

Change the bases and you may change the amino acids, the shape of the protein and what it can do. This one-base change causes sickle cell disease.

All 3D models and simulations: © Digital Vector · digitalvector.com.au. The beta-globin sequence is the start of the human HBB gene, shortened for teaching. Shapes of molecules are simplified.

Teacher notes

Two self-contained labs in one offline HTML file for grades 9–12 biology. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks and iPads included). Nothing is uploaded and no student data is collected.

Learning goals

Students will be able to:

  • Transcribe a DNA template strand into mRNA using the base-pairing rules.
  • Translate mRNA into a sequence of amino acids using a codon chart.
  • Describe the jobs of RNA polymerase, mRNA, tRNA and the ribosome.
  • Classify mutations as substitutions, insertions or deletions, and as silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift.
  • Explain how a single base change causes sickle cell disease.

Suggested sequence (2 class periods)

  • Lab 1 · Build a Protein (1 period): Transcription (students choose the RNA base for each template base; the first is a worked example), mRNA export, and translation with a clickable codon chart (the start codon is worked). Two genes: a 5-codon practice gene, then the first 8 codons of human beta-globin.
  • Lab 2 · Mutation Lab (1 period): Single-base substitutions, insertions and deletions; side-by-side comparison of original and mutant proteins; students name each mutation (silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift); the sickle cell mutation as a case study.

What the models assume

  • The beta-globin gene is the real start of human HBB (ATG GTG CAC CTG ACT CCT GAG GAG …) with a stop codon added after codon 8. Counting the starting Met as amino acid 1, the sickle cell change is at amino acid 7 (GAG → GTG, Glu → Val). Many textbooks call it position 6, because the first Met is removed from the finished protein.
  • RNA processing (introns, cap and tail), the promoter, and the three ribosome sites (A, P, E) are left out. Strand directions (5′ and 3′) are labeled but not tested.
  • In Lab 2 the start codon is locked, and one change is made at a time. A substitution that removes the stop codon is counted as missense (the protein runs on into the bases after the gene).

Misconceptions these labs target

  • “mRNA has the same letters as the template strand.” Copying the template base is marked wrong, with feedback on pairing.
  • “RNA contains T.” Choosing T is corrected: RNA uses U.
  • “DNA leaves the nucleus to make protein.” Only the mRNA passes through the nuclear pore.
  • “Each amino acid has exactly one codon.” Silent mutations work because most amino acids have several codons.
  • “All mutations are harmful, and all are inherited.” Students make silent mutations, and a question separates body-cell from egg and sperm mutations.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-LS1-1 (Construct an explanation for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins, which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.). Supports HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-2. Practices: Developing and Using Models; Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions. Crosscutting concepts: Structure and Function; Cause and Effect.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42, adopted 2021): B.7A (identify the components of DNA and explain how the nucleotide sequence specifies some traits); B.7B (describe gene expression and explain protein synthesis using models of DNA and RNA); B.7C (identify and illustrate changes in DNA and evaluate the significance of these changes). Scientific and engineering practices: B.1G, B.2A, B.3A.
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.4 (determine the meaning of symbols, key terms and domain-specific words); RST.9-10.7 (translate information between words, tables, graphs and equations); WHST.9-10.2 (write informative and explanatory texts, including scientific procedures).
  • AP Biology (2025 course framework): 6.3 Transcription and RNA Processing; 6.4 Translation; 6.7 Mutations.

Safety and risk assessment

Using the simulation (screen only: no chemicals or equipment)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Screen useEye strain, poor postureEach lab fits one class period. Build in a short break; look away from the screen every 20 minutes.
Flashing or moving imagesPhotosensitivity, motion discomfortNo flashing or strobing content. The 3D camera moves only when the student moves it; fly-through moves become instant jumps when the device is set to reduce motion.
Student dataPrivacyRuns offline. No accounts, no tracking and nothing uploaded. Results stay in the browser on that device and can be cleared at any time.

Sensitive content

  • Sickle cell disease is used as the case study. Some students or their relatives may live with it. Present it factually, avoid singling anyone out, and note that it affects people of many backgrounds.

Accessibility

  • Every codon in the chart and every base in the DNA strand can be reached and chosen with the keyboard.
  • Bases are shown as letters as well as colors, and changed amino acids are marked with a ≠ sign.
  • All controls work with the keyboard: Tab to move, Enter or Space to press, arrow keys on sliders. In the 3D view, arrow keys rotate and the + and − keys zoom.
  • Gray controls cannot be used yet. They stay reachable and explain why when pressed.
  • Nothing is shown by color alone: right and wrong answers are marked ✓ and ✗, and results are given in words and numbers.
  • No sound, no flashing content, and no time limits that cannot be repeated. Text stays readable when the browser is zoomed to 200%.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan.
